theory.intro: A line of best fit is fitted to ALL the points in a dataset, so a single outlier — a point that sits well away from the main trend — can pull the line away from the pattern shown by the rest of the data. Removing that outlier changes how steep the line is.
facts: An outlier lies far from the main trend of the other points, on either side of where the line of best fit would otherwise sit.
While the outlier is included, it pulls the line of best fit toward itself, which can flatten the gradient shown by the rest of the data.
Removing an outlier that was flattening the line lets the remaining points show their true, steeper trend — the gradient becomes steeper.
The outlier's effect on the gradient describes a change in STEEPNESS. An association that is positive can stay positive — just steeper — once the outlier is removed.
steps: Identify the outlier: the point that sits far from the trend of the other points
Decide which side of the line the outlier sits on, and whether it is pulling the line flatter
State how the gradient changes once the outlier is removed: steeper or less steep

foundation.solution_text:
Every other point lies close to the line, but one point sits far above it.
The outlier is $(1.5, 25)$ — much higher sales than expected for that level of spend.

The outlier lies above the trend of the other points, pulling the fitted line up at low spend and making it less steep than the main cluster suggests.
Removing it lets the line follow the main cluster's steeper upward trend.
The gradient would become steeper.

Every other point lies close to the line, but one point sits far below it.
The outlier is $(8.5, 9)$ — much lower sales than expected for that level of spend.

The outlier lies below the trend of the other points, pulling the fitted line down at high spend and making it less steep than the main cluster suggests.
Removing it lets the line follow the main cluster's steeper upward trend.
The gradient would become steeper.

A line of best fit is fitted to every point, including the outlier.
Because the outlier sits well above where the trend of the other points would put it, the line is pulled upward at the low-spend end to stay closer to the outlier.
This pulls the low end of the line up relative to the high end, which reduces the line's overall steepness.

A line of best fit is fitted to every point, including the outlier.
Because the outlier sits well below where the trend of the other points would put it, the line is pulled downward at the high-spend end to stay closer to the outlier.
This pulls the high end of the line down relative to the low end, which reduces the line's overall steepness.

development.solution_text:
In the Before plot, the line rises gently, pulled up at the low-spend end by the outlier.
In the After plot, the line rises much more sharply, following the trend of the remaining $8$ stores.
The gradient has become steeper, while staying positive.

In the Before plot, the line rises gently, pulled down at the high-spend end by the outlier.
In the After plot, the line rises much more sharply, following the trend of the remaining $8$ stores.
The gradient has become steeper, while staying positive.

Zara has the effect backwards.
The outlier is what is currently pulling the line's low end up and flattening it — the outlier is not helping the line rise, it is holding it down at high spend relative to the trend.
Removing the outlier removes this flattening influence, so the gradient becomes steeper, not less steep.

A single point that lies far from the trend of the rest of the data can still have a large effect on a line of best fit, especially when it sits near the edge of the spend range.
Even though it is only one of nine points, its distance from the trend gives it a strong pull on the fitted line.
Removing it noticeably steepens the gradient, even though it is only one point.

Both before and after removing the outlier, sales increase as spend increases, so the direction stays positive.
Only the steepness changes: the gradient becomes more positive (steeper), not negative.
Removing an outlier does not automatically flip the direction of an association that is already clearly shown by the rest of the data.

development.question_text: In one dataset, the outlier has low spend and high sales, sitting above the trend on the left. In another dataset, the outlier has high spend and low sales, sitting below the trend on the right. In both cases, removing the outlier makes the line of best fit steeper. Explain what these two outliers have in common that produces the same effect.
development.solution_text:
Both outliers sit on the side of the line that flattens it: one drags the low-spend end of the line up, the other drags the high-spend end of the line down.
Either way, the outlier's presence pulls the fitted line away from the steeper trend shown by the rest of the data.
Removing either outlier removes this flattening pull, so both cases give the same result: a steeper gradient.

mastery.question_text: After removing an outlier at $(1.5, 25)$ from a set of advertising spend and monthly sales data, the line of best fit passes through about $(1, 8)$ and $(9, 30)$ — a steep, positive gradient. What can you say about the ORIGINAL line of best fit, before the outlier was removed? Explain your reasoning.
mastery.solution_text:
At spend $=1.5$, the new (after-removal) line predicts sales of about $8 + 2.75(0.5) \approx 9.4$ thousand, but the outlier's actual sales were $25$ thousand — far above this prediction.
So the outlier had low spend but unusually high sales relative to the trend, and sat well above where the trend of the rest of the data would put it.
Including a point like this pulls the low-spend end of the line upward, which flattens the line relative to the steeper trend of the remaining points.
So the original line (with the outlier included) must have been less steep than the steep line seen after its removal.

mastery.question_text: A classmate says, "Once the outlier is removed, the new line of best fit must have a completely different direction — for example, changing from positive to negative." Using the advertising spend and sales scenario, explain why this claim is generally wrong.
mastery.solution_text:
Removing a single outlier rarely flips the overall direction shown by a clear cluster of the remaining points.
In this scenario, the $8$ remaining stores already show a clear, consistent positive trend on their own.
Removing the outlier keeps the line positive — it only makes the line steeper, not negative.

mastery.question_text: A third store's data point is an outlier at $(0.5, 2)$ — low spend AND low sales, sitting roughly along the same direction as the rest of the increasing trend, not far above or below the line itself. Would removing this point be likely to change the gradient much? Explain, referencing what makes an outlier influential.
mastery.solution_text:
This point is unusual in that it is far from the OTHER points, but it still lies close to where the line of best fit would already put it — it does not sit far above or below the line.
An outlier only distorts the gradient when it lies far from the line, not just far from the other points.
Because this point roughly follows the line's direction, removing it would have little effect on the gradient.
